title: Anahat Singh Fights Back to Beat Salma Hany, Reaches Maiden PSA Gold Semifinal
excerpt: A day after stunning Nour ElSherbini, the 18-year-old world No. 15 came from 2-1 down to beat the world No. 14 in five games at the Silicon Valley Open — and now gets a rematch with Asian Games champion Sivasangari Subramaniam.
body:
• Anahat Singh, 18, beat Egypt's Salma Hany 4-11, 11-8, 4-11, 11-2, 11-5 in 42 minutes at the Silicon Valley Open to reach her maiden PSA Gold-level semifinal.
  • The quarterfinal win came a day after she stunned eight-time world champion Nour ElSherbini in straight games — back-to-back victories over the world No. 3 and No. 14.
  • She now faces Malaysia's world No. 4 Sivasangari Subramaniam, who beat her in the Asian Games singles final last month — a rematch with a place in the final at stake.
  • Whatever happens next, the Redwood City run caps a landmark 2026: world junior champion (a first for India) and the first Indian woman to reach an Asian Games squash singles final.

Anahat Singh's California run is not done. A day after producing the biggest win of her career against Nour ElSherbini, the 18-year-old from Delhi fought back from 2-1 down to beat Egypt's sixth seed Salma Hany in five games on Thursday and reach the first PSA Gold-level semifinal of her career at the Silicon Valley Open in Redwood City.

The scoreline — 4-11, 11-8, 4-11, 11-2, 11-5 in 42 minutes — tells the shape of it. Hany, the world No. 14, took the first and third games and looked in control of the rallies; Anahat then dropped just seven points across the final two games, closing out the match with the kind of authority that has defined her week. It was the first meeting between the two players.

"I was a bit tired coming into the match because of the emotions after winning yesterday. I just didn't want to let go of the momentum today, I wanted to give it my all and I'm happy to get one step further in the tournament."

— Anahat Singh

Backing Up the ElSherbini Upset

Breakthrough wins are common in squash; backing them up 24 hours later is not. Anahat's straight-games dismissal of ElSherbini — the top seed, world No. 3 and winner of eight world titles — on Wednesday was the result of the tournament. The Hany win, reported by IANS and NationPress, converts it from a one-match story into a tournament run: the world No. 15 has now beaten two top-14 Egyptians in consecutive rounds at a USD 143,500 Gold event.

"I've never played her before, and I didn't know what to expect coming on to the court," Anahat said of Hany. "Especially after winning yesterday, I know that if I'm playing well I had a chance against whoever I played. I wanted to come in with that mindset."

A Rematch With History

The semifinal pairs her with Malaysia's Sivasangari Subramaniam, the world No. 4 and reigning Asian Games champion, who beat compatriot Rachel Arnold in straight games. The two met in the Asian Games women's singles final in Aichi-Nagoya last month, where Sivasangari won 3-0 and Anahat took silver — the first Indian woman to reach that final. The Malaysian's gold also booked her place at the Los Angeles Olympics, where squash makes its debut. Friday's semifinal is, in effect, an early audition for that Olympic stage.

The Year That Keeps Adding Firsts

Anahat arrived in California as the reigning world junior champion — earlier this year she became the first Indian to win the World Junior title, ending Egypt's 15-year hold on the crown — and with two Asian Games bronze medals from Hangzhou 2023 already upgraded to a 2026 singles silver. A Gold-event semifinal at 18, reached by beating the sport's most decorated active player and then a top-six seed, moves her from prospect to contender. The final is one win away; the final is on Saturday in Redwood City.
